#3334. IEEE Offers More Services to Cities That Want to Be Smarter

They include webinars, educational resources, and conferences

Georges Zissis is an IEEE Fellow and chair of the IEEE Smart Cities Technical Community.

Satish Sani is an IEEE senior member and chair of the IEEE Smart Grid Technical Track.

More and more city governments are using advanced technologies to improve livability for their residents. Municipalities use data from smartphones and sensors for traffic enforcement, traffic control, and waste management. They also have implemented artificial intelligence and deep learning programs.

Dubai, Paris, and Coral Gables, Fla., are among the cities that have invested heavily in programs to become smarter.

Although many initiatives have delivered real innovations, not all have been successful. Inefficient global coordination has hindered projects with unclear standards, socioeconomic differences, and a lack of worldwide governance, leading to a disconnect between the technologies and the ability to adapt to them.

Smart city projects are complex and expensive endeavors that involve politicians, citizens, technocrats, and engineers. Successful projects require citizens to be fully engaged and to have strong collaborations with the participants, especially engineers, as engineering is the cornerstone.

Collaboration with universities, research institutions, and technology experts can bridge knowledge gaps on the behavior of complex socio-technical systems. What’s missing, though, is a global platform where those involved can discuss their experiences.

To help solve those and other challenges, the IEEE Smart Cities Technical Community (formerly the IEEE Smart Cities Initiative) was launched in 2013 by IEEE Future Directions, which incubates emerging technologies and new applications of current ones. The technical community provides city leaders and others with credible, unbiased information and educational content developed by IEEE experts.

Since then, IEEE Smart Cities has launched services including its flagship International Smart Cities Conference, a media center with educational and technical resources, and a contest to recognize the best smart project completed by city officials. The platforms bring together practicing engineers, academic researchers, policymakers, and city leaders to collaborate and exchange ideas and experiences about moving toward a smart-city model.

In 2021 the IEEE Power & Energy Society began managing the Smart Cities program, which is supported by the IEEE Communications, Industry Applications, and Intelligent Transportation Systems societies and other IEEE entities.

Thanks to volunteers’ dedication and determination, IEEE Smart Cities launched several services. But the initiative’s structure limited the development of long-term projects and the creation of new activities.

To address the situation, the IEEE Technical Activities Board (TAB) created the second-generation technical community ad hoc committee, also in 2021. It was a pilot program whereby IEEE Smart Cities formed a board of governors to oversee the community’s operations and leadership, and created a policies and procedures manual.

In November 2025 IEEE Smart Cities became a TAB technical community.

Today more than 7,000 volunteers collaborate on various aspects of the community within at least one of the following technical tracks:

New webinar series, workshops, conferences, educational resources, and other offerings are being created.

Two events were launched recently: the IEEE European Technology and Engineering Management Summit, held in May 2025 in Belgium, with the next one planned for 2027; and the IEEE Sustainable Smart Lighting World Conference, scheduled for 2 to 6 December in Athens.

The Smart Cities Ambassadors program aims to raise the technical community’s visibility outside IEEE by holding roundtables and other events at non-IEEE functions.

IEEE Smart Cities volunteers are working on launching journals. In addition, standards are being developed in collaboration with the IEEE Standards Association, societies, and councils.

The program is collaborating with the Open and Agile Smart Cities and Communities network, the Instituto de Competitividad e Innovación para el Desarrollo y Transferencia de Tecnología, and the International Project Management Association.

All of those actions have the ultimate objective of boosting IEEE Smart Cities’ growth and sustainability, as well as strengthening the leadership and educational offerings to technical community volunteers.

If you would like to volunteer, visit the Smart Cities website.

Georges Zissis is an IEEE Fellow and chair of the IEEE Smart Cities Technical Community.

Satish Sani is an IEEE senior member and chair of the IEEE Smart Grid Technical Track.

#3331. tvOS 27.2 adds new Apple TV 4K setting that’s an instant favorite

tvOS 27.2 launched last week as the latest software update for Apple TV 4K, and it includes a new setting I’m a big fan of: Shuffle for screen savers.

Screen savers have been one of the best Apple TV features since tvOS first launched in 2015. Largely that’s due to the gorgeous aerials captured around the world (and even from space).

Aerials are still my favorite type of Apple TV screen saver, but tvOS has steadily added other categories worth checking out too.

Currently inside Settings ⇾ Screen Saver you’ll find four categories:

The second and third options tap into your Apple Photos library and introduce the joy of seeing your favorite memories pop up on the big screen. Snoopy screen savers feature the beloved Peanuts character in a variety of entertaining scenes.

All of these screen saver options are great. But until tvOS 27.2, you had to select just one category and that’s all you’d ever see.

Now with tvOS 27.2, Apple has introduced a ‘Shuffle’ option that randomly cycles through screen savers from across all four categories.

It’s a welcome new setting, long overdue but I’ve been enjoying it a lot. The ability to be surprised by more different screen savers may sound like a small thing, but it’s a meaningful improvement to the Apple TV 4K experience.

Have you tried the new Shuffle setting for screen savers in tvOS 27.2? Let us know in the comments.

#3329. This Hidden Device Could Free Up Gigawatts of Grid Power

Variable frequency drives can slash motors’ power use

Zurich-based ABB is one of several manufacturers of variable frequency drives (VFDs), such as this ACH580. VFDs could help make the millions of electric motors running in industrial facilities more energy efficient.

This article was originally published by Canary Media.

America’s energy supply crunch is driving a surge of federal and private investment in new electricity generation—from polluting gas turbines to cleaner developments like solar farms and geothermal plants. But gigawatts of power are already available for the taking across the U.S. economy in the form of wasted energy from an unexpected source: motors.

Some 50 million electric motors drive the fans, pumps, and compressors found in virtually every factory and building. Together, they gobble enough electricity to equal nearly a third of total U.S. power demand. Often, the motors use far more energy than they actually need to keep America’s machines humming.

Companies can install devices known as variable frequency drives, or VFDs, to make motors run super efficiently. Yet adoption remains relatively low, in part because of the perceived hassle of retrofitting equipment and because they’re typically not required. On average, only 16 percent of motor systems at industrial facilities and 4 percent of commercial-sector motors use VFDs, according to a 2021 market report by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

However, there are now more reasons than ever to equip the nation’s motors with power-saving devices, energy experts and device manufacturers say. They’re urging federal agencies, utilities, and deep-pocketed tech giants to spur a wider rollout of VFDs through financial incentives and efficiency standards.

For one, slashing motors’ power use would free up grid capacity for large electricity users like data centers and electric vehicles, they argue. It would help curb costs for factories that are switching from fossil-fueled heating systems to electrified, motor-based solutions like heat pumps—all at a time when industrial power prices are climbing fast. Plus, VFD technology has become far more sophisticated and less expensive to install than earlier iterations.

“This is low-hanging fruit that gives a lot [of energy] back and is reasonably simple,” Nik Sawe, a senior policy analyst at the nonpartisan think tank Energy Innovation, says of the technology.

Energy-wise, the main problem with electric motors is that they’re always running at full capacity. Consider an office building, which empties out in the evening. The heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning system can wind down in those hours, with dampers and valves restricting the flow of cold or hot air. But the motors and fans that drive the whole setup are still working in the background, wasting energy.

VFD technology, such as the Danfoss iC7 series, has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings trying to combat rising electricity costs. Danfoss Drives

VFDs are electronic controllers with temperature sensors that continually adjust the speed of motors, automatically ramping up or down to match demand. The technology, which is also called adjustable speed drives, has the potential to curb a motor’s energy use by around 40 to 60 percent, says Neal Elliott, director emeritus of the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy.

All those energy reductions add up. Toyota, for example, installed VFDs on over 200 motors inside the HVAC system at its auto manufacturing plant in Georgetown, Kentucky, as part of a US $1.25 million pilot project in 2015. The automaker saved more than $700,000 in annual electricity costs thanks to the VFDs, and it continues to use the technology at other manufacturing facilities across the U.S., the company said by email.

“We’ve known for many, many years that there’s a huge opportunity for energy savings by varying the speed of the motor,” says Elliott, who noted that he literally wrote the book on energy-efficient motor systems in 2002.

Certain aspects of the technology have historically held the drives back since they debuted in the late 1960s. Measuring the flow of water, air, refrigerant—whatever is moving through the system that the motors are driving—was for decades an expensive engineering process. Accurately controlling motors to deliver the right amount of juice, at just the right time, faced similar issues.

But recent advances in sensors and machine-learning algorithms have significantly slashed the cost and complexity of using drives, Elliott says. Modern VFDs have also benefited from the increased production of advanced power chips that are used in high-voltage applications such as electric vehicles and solar power inverters.

Another long-standing challenge has been that commercial and industrial building developers often prioritize reducing upfront costs over netting long-term energy savings, and so they don’t always build to the highest efficiency levels, says Zack Valdez, senior director of regulatory and industry affairs at the National Electrical Manufacturers Association, whose members include drive and motor makers.

“If the facility that you’re putting it into doesn’t require it, then oftentimes people will overlook [VFDs], because they’re just trying to build to a minimum set of energy requirements,” he says. And if companies don’t install drives from the start, they’re likely less inclined to take time to retrofit an operating system.

The trade association recently launched a pilot program with manufacturers, utilities, and energy-efficiency groups to collect real-world data about how VFDs reduce motors’ electricity use and lower utility bills. The goal is to demonstrate how the technology can benefit not only individual facilities but also the wider grid—giving utilities a concrete reason to provide rebates for industrial customers.

Proponents say they hope the results will help the U.S. Department of Energy shape future efficiency measures and incentives that encourage adoption of the drives, including in federally owned buildings. Despite the Trump administration’s open hostility toward home appliance and equipment mandates, agency staff have apparently been receptive to discussing solutions that could meet the soaring power needs of data centers.

“If you added a drive to all the motors that are out there, you could provide [power for] up to five years of data center growth without having to build any new generation,” says Kirk Anderson, director of government relations and public affairs for ABB. The global manufacturing giant makes VFDs domestically near Milwaukee.

Anderson floated the idea of having tech companies help pay for factory owners to install VFDs to free up room on the grid. After all, hyperscalers are already spending many billions of dollars to revive shuttered nuclear plants, support next-generation geothermal projects, deploy fleets of grid-scale batteries, and supercharge the build-out of gas turbines and power plants.

“Instead of ‘bring your own power,’ it should be ‘offset your own power,’” he says, referring to a growing effort by states to get data centers to secure their own power resources and prevent rising costs for regular customers.

Michael Reckamp, the director of enterprise strategy for Danfoss Drives, North America, another VFD manufacturer, said that despite the traditionally low adoption rates, the technology has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings as rising electricity costs and other grid-wide challenges make it harder to justify wasting energy.

Still, “it hasn’t permeated enough to get everyone utilizing it,” he says. “In the current situation, where we’re having so many issues with grids, brownouts, and now data centers wanting to take the load, I think there should be a renewed focus on putting drives out there to really reduce the stress on the grid and improve energy savings.”

Maria Gallucci is a clean-energy reporter with Canary Media.

Thank you for pointing out this accessible opportunity. I wonder why the industrial and non-residential building sectors still haven’t implemented this technology on a broad scale. The variable frequency drive (VFD) technology is very mature, widely available, and not new. It’s such a low-hanging fruit to implement wherever there are rotating machines and actuators to save energy, money, and also make the whole integrated energy system potentially more flexible and efficient.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind everyone that today's conference call will contain forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 and other securities laws.

These forward-looking statements are based on the company's expectations and beliefs as of today, November 5, 2026. Forward-looking statements are subject to risks and uncertainties that may cause actual results to differ materially from those projected. The company undertakes no obligation to provide updates or revisions to the forward-looking statements made in today's call. Additional information concerning factors that could cause those differences is contained in our filings with the SEC and in the press release announcing our results. Investors are cautioned not to place undue reliance on any forward-looking statements. Further, please note that we may refer to certain non-GAAP financial information on today's call.

You can find reconciliations of the non-GAAP financial measures to the most comparable GAAP measures in our earnings press release. Today's call is being recorded and will be available for replay. With that, I'll hand the call over to Casey Crenshaw for his remarks.

J. Crenshaw: Thank you, Andy, and good morning to everyone joining us today. Our third quarter results were in line with our expectations and consistent with the outlook we provided on our call last quarter. Revenue improved 25% sequentially and adjusted EBITDA improved to $1.9 million. Following the conclusion of multiple large contracts at the end of 2025, we have now turned the corner with momentum continuing to build ahead of what we expect will be a record 2027 for Stabilis. The driver of the sequential improvement from the second quarter was the short-term behind-the-meter power generation contract we secured earlier this year to support the commissioning of a U.S. data center. We began delivering LNG under the agreement in August.

As a result, data center-related revenue represented 17% of our total revenue in the third quarter compared to less than 1% in the second quarter. This project will conclude in the fourth quarter. Looking ahead, our focus is squarely on 2027. Our multiyear agreement to supply LNG for behind-the-meter bridge power at a U.S. data center expected to be the largest contract to date in our company's history remains on track to begin in the first quarter of 2027 and will ramp during the second and third quarters. We are progressing as planned on the pre-commissioning for the project with more than $15 million of specific project equipment on order and scheduled for delivery ahead of start-up.

The investment required for the readiness is fully funded by customer advanced payments under the contract. We are also finalizing LNG supply agreements for the project, along with backup supply alternatives to support reliable delivery. Beyond the contracts in hand, demand for small-scale LNG to support behind-the-meter power at data centers remains robust. We think about these opportunities in 4 phases: construction, commissioning, bridge power and long-term backup. Our commercial team is bidding on additional work across multiple phases of data center demand. We believe we are well positioned to extend our growth runway well beyond 2027 and the contract that begins next year. Outside of the data center market, aerospace remains the other key growth engine of our business.

Revenue from aerospace customers increased 49% year-over-year in the third quarter, driven by the increasing pace of launch and testing activity and a growing number of commercial space customers. These customers have demanding purity and delivery requirements and the operating track record we have built with them is difficult to replicate. We are currently in discussions with multiple space customers for long-term offtake agreements. Turning to Galveston. We continue to engage with prospective customers and financing partners, and we believe the project offers an attractive long-term growth opportunity for Stabilis. That said, we are not ready to commit to a time line for FID, which remains subject to arranging a final financing structure and securing sufficient commercial offtake.

While we remain super excited about the long-term value of the project and what it could and we believe will create, our primary short-term and near-term growth opportunities remain in the aerospace and behind-the-meter data center power projects. To close, the third quarter marked the beginning of a transformational period for Stabilis. While fourth quarter revenues will reflect the conclusion of our short-term data center project, we expect meaningful revenue growth in 2027. We have returned to profitability on a net income basis. Our largest contract is funded and on schedule, and our growth end markets are expanding.

We expect this momentum to build in 2027, and we remain committed to delivering value for our customers and our shareholders through disciplined capital allocation and focused execution. With that, I'll turn the call over to Andy for a detailed review of our financials.

Andrew Puhala: Thank you, Casey. I'll begin with a discussion of our third quarter performance, followed by an update on our cash flow, balance sheet, liquidity and capital spending. Third quarter revenue was $14.8 million, a decrease of 27% compared to the third quarter of 2025. Similar to the first 2 quarters of the year, the year-over-year decline reflects the completion of large marine and power generation contracts in the fourth quarter of 2025, partially offset by continued growth in aerospace, where revenue increased 49% compared to the prior year period as well as growth in our legacy industrial business. On a sequential basis, revenue increased $2.9 million or 25% from $11.9 million in the second quarter.

That increase was primarily driven by the short-term data center contract that began deliveries in August, which took data center-related revenue from less than 1% of the total in the second quarter to 17% in the third. Adjusted EBITDA was $1.9 million in the third quarter compared to $2.9 million in the prior year period, with the decrease attributable to the completion of the 2 large multiyear contracts in the fourth quarter of 2025. Sequentially, adjusted EBITDA increased to $1.9 million from $0.1 million in the second quarter, primarily due to the higher revenues.

Net income was $0.2 million or $0.01 per diluted share compared to net income of $1.1 million in the third quarter of 2025 and a net loss of $4.6 million in the second quarter. I would also note that SG&A was $2.5 million in the quarter, essentially flat with the second quarter and down from $2.8 million a year ago. Turning to cash flow. Operating cash flow was $3.9 million in the third quarter compared to $2.4 million a year ago and included a $5 million customer advance payment for our 2027 data center contract. Second quarter operating cash flow was $7.1 million, which also included a $5 million advance payment.

So the sequential decline primarily reflects changes in working capital. Year-to-date, cash flow from operations totaled $23.4 million, reflecting the full $25 million of advanced payments we've now received under the contract. At quarter end, cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash totaled $18.4 million compared to $18.9 million at the end of the second quarter. Of the $18.4 million, $16.8 million is restricted to support equipment purchases and other preparations for the 2027 data center contract and $1.5 million is unrestricted. Capital expenditures totaled $4 million during the quarter compared to $2.3 million in the second quarter, bringing year-to-date capital spending to $11.5 million. These expenditures were primarily related to equipment and infrastructure for the upcoming data center contract.

Looking ahead, we expect to continue investing to secure equipment and guaranteed supply ahead of the first quarter 2027 start, and we expect those investments to continue to be funded by the advanced payments already received. Before I close, a brief reminder on the points we made last quarter about the earnings profile of the business as we continue to scale. Nothing here is new, and we're not providing 2027 guidance, but with the third quarter now behind us, they're worth keeping in mind. First, our fixed cost base is largely in place, and we do not expect those costs to grow in proportion to revenue as the 2027 contract comes online, which should drive meaningful operating leverage.

Second, we'll service much of the incremental power generation demand with third-party LNG, so it requires limited incremental capital and preserves our plant capacity to support continued growth with our aerospace and other existing customers. The equipment for the 2027 contract is being funded by advanced payments already received. And third, our contracts pass through all commodity price risk. Taken together and in the context of a materially larger revenue base in 2027, this should translate into meaningful growth in adjusted EBITDA dollars and margin expansion into the high-teens as execution accelerates. That concludes our prepared remarks. Operator, please open the line for the Q&A session.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question is coming from Martin Malloy with Johnson Rice.

Martin Malloy: First question, I just wanted to ask about the aerospace market, and it sounded -- in your prepared remarks sounded incrementally positive on what's going on there. Could you maybe talk a little bit more about the volumes involved with these discussions with customers for long-term offtake contracts versus your current business and perhaps could this lead to investments in additional liquefaction capacity?

J. Crenshaw: Yes. Let me start, Marty. And again, thanks for joining the call today and covering the company. And I'll take it from a high level and then let Andy try to come in and answer anything additional. But look, we just -- if we didn't -- if we weren't clear, we believe Stabilis has 3 really dynamic markets that we operate in. One is the behind-the-meter power business that works in hyperscaler data centers, just distributed power markets, like all types of different end markets. Second is this giant marine bunkering infrastructure opportunity. And finally, it's the aerospace business that we've been heavily involved with since, I guess, 2018, 2019, quite some time.

And we provide high purity, reliable supply to people in the aerospace, primarily related to rockets and launching rockets primarily for telecommunications, satellites, different things of the nature. We don't know exactly everything they do, but mainly those end markets. And we are just seeing the maturing of the business with both additional customers, so more clients that are real clients that buy product and need product and the expansion and increasing the launching and testing by all of those clients.

And so that both expansion of the customer base and maturing of the customer base and the increased activity of all the customers across that industry is driving the growth and our historic performance is leading us to be successful in some of the market. We certainly don't have all of anything, but we have proximity to some clients and historical relationships with others, and we expect it to be a meaningful growth area for us. One of the challenges with the customers is due to the newness of some of the programs, you have anomalies, you have changes in timing, you have regulatory stuff that everybody is going through.

So that changes some of the visibility of cadence of everything, but we're starting to see clients ask for multiyear offtake arrangements, and we're having multiple customers that were involved with that. At the same time, there's conversations out there about some of the clients wanting to vertically integrate. So you have a lot of noise out there, but the growth is kind of beyond any of the negative noise out there. So I touched it from a high, high level, and then I'll let Andy add to it if there's anything to add. But we expect it to continue to grow, to continue to grow as a -- in volume and revenue.

As a percentage of the overall company, when you see the new behind-the-meter activity that's contracted, that may grow -- as you look at percentages, that may just outgrow that growth rate next year, but we're seeing some tremendous growth rate and multiyear contracting happening in the aerospace industry. Your last question was, will we have enough demand or term contracts to add capacity? And we think we hope to and if they want to contract that, we're in some discussions to add infrastructure and capacity. We've talked about contracting with -- even in the Galveston facility to bring it inbound in land from there. We've talked about additional expansion opportunities with infrastructure.

So we're actively involved with that, but we don't have anything to give you any forward guidance on that other than multiple customers now, multiple term contracting negotiations going on. So real positive overall market movement.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Barry Haimes with Sage Asset Management.

Barry Haimes: Congrats on the quarter. I had a couple of questions. One is the new data center contract that's starting up in the first quarter, is there an end date to that or just a little bit more feel for the term there? That's the first question. I have a couple of others, but that's the first one.

J. Crenshaw: Well, first of all, thanks for being on the call. It's a multiyear contract. I'll let Andy give the details of what we can go over on that.

Andrew Puhala: Yes, Barry. What we've disclosed publicly is that it's roughly a $200 million contract over 2 years, and it will ramp starting at beginning of next year. Now it's bridge power, so a lot of these bridge power contracts depend on when the data center gets their permanent connection. So the initial contracts for 2 years, I think it is possible that, that gets extended depending on the timing of grid connections and that sort of thing, but we just don't know yet.

Barry Haimes: Got it. Okay. Second question, could you give a little more of an update on the marine market? And do you still have the cruise customer you used to have? And just a little bit more color on that market.

J. Crenshaw: Yes. So I'll take it from a high level and then let Andy come in after that. But the cruise or I should say, marine bunkering business is something we've been doing. We've talked about it a lot. We have a specific project that we've talked a lot about in the Houston Ship Channel, specifically Galveston related to a couple of different cruise customer opportunities. We have one contract in hand with a long-term customer relationship.

And when you look at the macro right now and you look at the alternatives of our really strong, high creditworthy cruise customers, they can either use marine gas oil, which is kind of a diesel-based product or LNG and their ships have switching capability. And because of the disruptions globally and the increased cost around those alternatives, there need for a fit-for-purpose asset to make LNG molecules and then have fit-for-purpose delivery capability and bunkering vessel is high. And the macro is better than it's ever been for us to get an asset financed with enough adequate offtake to help that process happen.

And one of the challenges with this offtake agreements to get the project financing is the duration of contracting and how the contracting works to make the project financing work. This project is a $350 million total project, and it requires significant committed offtake over a significant amount of time to make the project financing work for everybody. And so we're just working through those processes, but the macro is really strong on moving that project forward. And Stabilis' project is the furthest along and we believe the most efficiently cost process in the Gulf Coast region. And so we believe we're the leader of the pack in that area, but we still haven't gotten the project to final FID.

Barry Haimes: Okay. Great. And just one quick follow-up on that. Is the -- in terms of how much offtake is committed, I mean, just ballpark it, is it 1/3 committed half, 2/3? Like just where are you in that process? What inning are we in, if you will?

J. Crenshaw: Yes. Well, right now, we've got about 25% of the committed offtake that we -- of that facility, the 350,000 gallons a day production. We don't need 100% offtake, but we need more than what we have now.

Barry Haimes: Got it. Fair enough. And then just last question. The 3 key markets you mentioned, behind-the-meter, the marine bunkering and the aerospace, could you give a rough sense of what percent of revenues each of those were? And where do you think it's most representative, either the third quarter just reported, year-to-date estimate for '27, what -- I'm not looking for precision. I'm just looking for a ballpark.

J. Crenshaw: Yes. Let me give you the ballpark real quick. I think the best thing to do is to think about '27 and '28 where we have booked and contracted right now. So we've already disclosed that we're assuming -- we have one contract that's a $200 million contract, plus or minus, think about $100 million in revenue a year. We have other behind-the-meter power opportunities that we are bidding and actively working on and intend to execute on. And then we have the aerospace market, which is growing really fast, but a lower base when you think about percentages of growth rate.

And then you talk about marine, where we really see marine being very strong for Stabilis is out past not next year, but hopefully getting some real revenue and earnings back during 2028. And when you look at the 10 years past there, we're really excited about that being an anchor term duration while we have up and downs from both aerospace and behind-the-meter projects. So that is not perfectly clear explanation, but we see short term, those kind of percentages happening.

And then when you look 3 years out and further and you start talking about how that backup power on behind-the-meter demand starts happening where you need like peaking opportunities with LNG around large behind-the-meter projects, and you continue to see the aerospace growing, those can be major, major long-term contributors consistent. And -- but obviously, once we get the asset in on the -- an FID the marine project, that will be a meaningful percentage of revenue at that point in time. But that's not in our kind of next year plan, which we expect to be a record year for Stabilis.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Matt Dhane with Tieton Capital Management.

Matthew Dhane: I had a couple of questions here. First one, the data center contract that starts here in Q1 of '27. Just was looking for a little bit more detail. Does that start January time frame? Does it start later in the quarter? And then secondarily, please confirm I heard correctly, so it ramps over Q2, Q3. So does that imply that Q4 is finally the full run rate for that contract?

Andrew Puhala: Yes. Matt, I appreciate you joining the call today. So second question first, it will ramp over the first 3 quarters of the year. And so by the fourth quarter of next year, yes, we expect that to be kind of at the full run rate. In terms of start-up, it will start middle of the first quarter. It will start with mobilization of equipment and testing and some things like that. And then the deliveries will start to -- the LNG deliveries will start to ramp from there. So that's kind of the schedule and really the level of detail that we can go into at this point.

Matthew Dhane: Okay. Great. Appreciate that, Andy. Then also I want to get a little bit more color, if I could, on the pipeline of data center opportunities. I know you talked about the 4 different buckets that they fall in. Just was curious, how would you -- I guess first off, classify the overall pipeline. Does it continue to grow or is it pretty much stable with what you saw last quarter? And then what is the largest bucket where a lot of those opportunities fall into? I assume bridge would be the largest just because of the size of the contract.

But just yes, if you could add more color where things tend to fall within the pipeline, that would be helpful.

J. Crenshaw: I'll try to give a little color. I don't know that we can give just all the detail around our kind of sales funnel. But I would say the first 3 categories are the biggest. That's the construction where they're trying -- to try to get wean themselves off diesel. That's a really good opportunity where we're doing the customer education and trying to show them how that's working. The commissioning has become kind of a new and now robust area where they're like we need to get the construction and the projects commissioned even before they get permanent power solutions in.

And bridge is becoming -- the size of bridge is pretty extreme, and it's not something that the customers are kind of anticipating. So it's becoming kind of a more and more needed area when they have disruptions on their time schedules on getting their grid connections or pipeline interconnections into the facility. So that's becoming a more and more needed issue as you see delays or unexpected things happen. The one that we're probably most -- seeing the most activity in the last quarter, and we think in the future is going to be this backup area where we're providing kind of backup solutions long term for our clients that are active in behind-the-meter activity around data centers.

And so that's the newest area that we're starting to see ramped up activity and questions around. Super excited about that. So I'd say if you talk about like increased activity, that's the most -- that's the one increasing the most. And then I'd say next increasing is just the bridge activity due to delays and so many projects coming online and having connection delays. So I hope I answered it without giving the specifics. All 4 of those areas are active and exciting to us.

And obviously, with the price of diesel and the intent on having environmental compliance with construction being a focus of communities, having LNG and a better environmental footprint on construction is important to the owners of the facilities.

Matthew Dhane: Okay. That is helpful. The overall size of the pipeline as of the end of the quarter or here today relative to, say, what it was like 3 to 6 months ago, let's say, 3 months ago, how would you say that? Does it just continue to increase the opportunities that you are bidding and talking to people about?

J. Crenshaw: Correct, substantially. I mean, a pipeline, you don't get to do -- you don't get to bill against a pipeline. The pipeline is a pipeline. So I'm talking -- there's significant projects out there. We do not have to land all of the -- very many of the opportunities to be super successful in this area, this growth area of our company. So that's the way we're kind of looking at this area. The opportunities are pretty, pretty extreme. There's a broad, deep need for infrastructure and execution in this space.

I'd say we're a little bit more tighter focused in marine, where we're much more focused on a specific project in a specific region where this area is pulling us into just where they're having issues on behind-the-meter or where they think they have a cost advantage.

Matthew Dhane: Understood. I hope you win more than your fair share.

J. Crenshaw: We are hoping to win enough to make our shareholders happy.

Operator: This concludes the Q&A portion of today's call. I would now like to turn the floor over to Andy Puhala for closing remarks.

Andrew Puhala: Well, thank you, everyone, for joining the call today. We appreciate your time and your continued interest and support of Stabilis. If you'd like to learn more, please reach out to me at our Investor Relations contact numbers, and we'll be happy to talk further. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. This concludes today's Stabilis Solutions Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. Please disconnect your line at this time, and have a wonderful day.

#3327. Anthropic upgrades Claude with new Personal Finance feature

Having the right context is what makes AI tools useful. Anthropic just launched the ability to securely use personal finance data with Claude. The company emphasizes that the feature is read-only and can’t take financial actions.

“Getting answers about your money no longer means opening every banking app and doing the math yourself,” Anthropic says. “With Personal Finance in Claude, you can securely connect your bank and card accounts and ask in your own words. Access is read-only, and Personal Finance can’t move, manage, or invest your money.”

Similar to ChatGPT’s finances feature, Claude’s new capabilities essentially give you a way to use chat as a way to make sense of your finance data. It can also present data in dashboards, calendars, and more.

Given the importance of security, here’s what Anthropic has to say regarding the new finance feature and Claude:

Claude’s access is read-only. Personal Finance helps you understand your money, and it isn’t designed to give investment advice. Claude can make mistakes in its answers, so ask which transactions are behind a number, and check important figures with your bank.

Your accounts are only connected once you sign in to your bank yourself through Plaid, a service that connects apps to banks. That’s where you agree to its terms and approve Claude’s read-only access, so Claude doesn’t ask for or see your bank password.

Smart city deployments have historically relied on cameras, sensors, and dashboards that capture data without delivering timely insight. Edge AI changes this by letting inference happen close to where data is generated. This supports faster decisions, stronger data sovereignty, and lower operating costs than cloud-only designs. This guide traces the progression from automation and perception to prediction, agentic coordination, and physical AI, where urban systems continuously perceive conditions, reason about them, and act within a tiered edge architecture spanning far-edge sensors, regional infrastructure, and the cloud. It also outlines the durability, security, and interoperability requirements that production-grade edge hardware and software must meet to support public safety, mobility, and infrastructure use cases at city scale.

#3325. Apple TV unveils return of hit comedy from Ted Lasso, Shrinking creator

Bad Monkey, an Apple TV comedy from the creator of Ted Lasso and Shrinking, returns soon for a new season. Here’s the just-released trailer for Bad Monkey season 2.

One of the biggest hitmakers at Apple TV is undoubtedly Bill Lawrence, co-creator of a trio of acclaimed comedies: Ted Lasso, Shrinking, and Bad Monkey.

Among the three, the Vince Vaughn-starring Bad Monkey is likely the one you’ve never heard of. But now is a perfect time to get caught up.

Bad Monkey season 2 debuts Wednesday, December 2 with one episode, followed by weekly releases through February 3.

Here’s Apple’s official plot summary, followed by the new trailer:

After Andrew Yancy (Vaughn) witnesses the murder of Florida’s finest fixer, an ambitious state attorney pairs him up with a strait-laced forensic accountant to solve the crime. Yancy finds himself embroiled in a turf war between rival criminal organizations as he navigates a variety of Florida oddballs, including an erudite mob boss, his unhinged son and a hard-edged young woman who needs Yancy’s protection. Meanwhile, Yancy contends with his aging father; unresolved romantic tension with Dr. Rosa Campesino (Natalie Martinez), who launches her own investigation into a mysterious rash; and a bombastic animal relocation specialist whose business threatens the local environment.

Joining several returning season 1 cast members is prominent addition John Malkovich. Malkovich plays a Miami mob boss that Vaughn’s Yancy finds himself up against.

You can watch Bad Monkey season 1 here on Apple TV.

Are you a fan of Bad Monkey? If you haven’t seen it yet, do you plan to watch? Let us know in the comments.

Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month, or you can get it discounted through the Apple One bundle.

'Primetime,' 'Resident Evil,' 'Possible Love,' and more movie night hits just landed on streaming

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

With spooky season in the rearview mirror, we're barreling through November at a steady clip, and another weekend ahead of us means the question of what to watch is fresh on our mind. Luckily, this week came with a wave of premieres on the best streaming services, so you're spoiled for choice.

Over on paid video-on-demand platforms, two of the biggest movies of the year — Robert Pattinson's queasy and mesmerizing turn in "Primetime" and Zach Cregger's surprisingly hilarious "Resident Evil" adaptation — are both available to stream from the comfort of your catch. For fans of "You Can See Everything," Netflix has a new drama called "Possible Love" that scratches the same itch.

So without further ado, let's dive into all the best new movies on streaming this weekend.

Robert Pattinson's been everywhere you look this year, but if you only see one of his blockbusters, I can't recommend "Primetime" enough. Director Lance Oppenheim turns a real-life media scandal into a neo-gothic nightmare that oozes style in every frame. Pattinson is delightfully unnerving as Chris Hansen, the host of the controversial reality series “To Catch a Predator,” which became infamous for its televised sting operations of suspected child predators.

Hansen seems almost giddy about the prospect of publicly shaming his targets, but as he and ambitious producer Andie Bender (Merritt Wever) push for bigger ratings, the public spectacle drowns out any moral standing they might have started with. It all turns into a queasy yet hypnotic critique of our obsession with reality TV, and a chilling reminder that sometimes the people behind the camera are just as terrifying as those in front of it.

Buy or rent "Primetime" on Amazon or Apple now

We're in a golden age of video game movie adaptations, and nowhere was that more on display than in Zach Cregger's new "Resident Evil" movie. Even if you've never played the games, you should still check out this tightly woven and surprisingly hilarious thriller with some of the best monster designs I've seen in years. Austin Abrams had a direct line to my funny bone as Bryan, our bumbling protagonist and audience avatar stuck with taking a package into Raccoon City.

Along the way, he crashes into a bloody woman standing in the middle of the road — and that ends up being the least weird thing that happens all night. He finds himself in the middle of a viral outbreak caused by the Umbrella Corporation, and he's unwittingly holding onto the only cure. He'll have to dodge armies of the horribly mutated undead to have any hope of getting out of this nightmare alive.

Buy or rent "Resident Evil" on Amazon or Apple now

If you were fascinated by "You Can See Everything," then Netflix's new drama from acclaimed Korean filmmaker Lee Chang-dong needs to be on your radar. It's not a documentary, but it is a fictional drama about a documentary that chews over many of the same questions about unreliable narrators and how much we can really trust filmmakers to tell us the truth.

Jeon Do-yeon stars as a a working-class woman named Mi-ok whose husband, Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), was one of several auto plant workers laid off after a union strike where authorities beat and killed workers. Mi-ok befriends a documentary filmmaker Lee Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong) and agrees to be in a documentary about the declining state of labor in South Korea. But as the two get closer, it becomes less and less clear what's real chemistry and what's a show put on for the cameras.

"Bourne" director Paul Greengrass's new historical action epic "The Uprising" stars Andrew Garfield as a grieving farm who gets swept up in a growing revolt against King Richard II. Fed up with crushing taxes and the crown's mistreatment of ordinary people, he helps rally thousands of commoners into an army and leads them on a march toward London.

It all culminates in a bloody clash as the rebels fight for justice against the powers that be. A compelling supporting cast adds plenty of weight to the story, while its brutal fight scenes and medieval setting make it an entertaining watch for anyone looking to get a better understanding on this period of history — or to simply lose yourself in a story from a bygone era.

Spooky season might be over and gone, but I'm still going to take every opportunity to plug quality horror movies that I can get. “The Wolf of Snow Hollow” is an offbeat genre mashup written, directed by, and starring Jim Cummings that feels equal parts procedural thriller and creature feature — with a wicked sense of humor to boot.

When a series of brutal killings shock a small town, the locals start to suspect a supernatural predator may be at play given that all the new bodies only ever show up after a full moon. The local sheriff John (Cummings) is determined to find a logical explanation, but as the body count rises and suspicion spreads through the community, the evidence points to some increasingly bizarre explanations.

Apple has released the first iOS 27.3 public beta for iPhone. The update brings back the redesigned Health app that briefly appeared during iOS 27.2 testing. It also adds vertical tabs in Safari, gives Siri AI more to do across Apple’s apps, and makes the iPhone Duo easier to use with one hand.

Apple released the first iOS 27.3 developer beta on November 3. The biggest change is the redesigned Health app, which didn’t make it into the final iOS 27.2 release.

On iPhones that support Apple Intelligence, the new Insights tab brings together trends from sleep, activity, and more. The Longevity tab includes Health Age, which uses Apple Watch data to show how your health metrics compare with what’s typical for your age.

For more changes, check out our full iOS 27.3 beta 1 roundup.

Back up your iPhone, then sign up for the free Apple Beta Software Program with the same Apple Account you use on your iPhone.

Go to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates and select iOS 27 Public Beta. Return to Software Update and tap Update Now when iOS 27.3 appears. If you’re already on the public beta track, you can check for the update directly in Software Update.

Some very high profile apps look downright awful

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I like to think I’m a patient person, but now that we’re two weeks after the iPhone Duo release date, I’m starting to wonder what the heck is going on with the app situation.

It’s not like the iPhone Duo doesn’t have other issues, whether it’s “Crackgate,” the weighty design, or the lack of a telephoto zoom. But my biggest issue right now has nothing to do with Apple or the hardware.

Don’t get me wrong; there are plenty of apps that have already been updated and optimized for Apple’s first foldable phone. Some of my favorite iPhone Duo apps include YouTube TV, which allows you to watch four shows at once in a grid view, the PianoFold Rhythm game, and AirMail with its handy 2-column layout.

But overall I’m pretty shocked by how many high-profile apps still look awful on the $2,000 iPhone Duo 2. Here are some of the worst offenders, and I’m warning you now that several are from Google.

I use Google Drive all of the time for uploading photos and reviewing documents, but I simply don’t want to on the iPhone Duo because it’s so visually jarring. There are huge black bars on the left and right on the 7.6-inch display, and the buttons to rotate and enlarge the view don’t really help.

You would think that spreadsheets would look way better on the iPhone Duo’s main screen. And they would if the app was actually optimized. Instead, you get the same black bars here as in the Google Drive app, and you have to scroll a lot to see content. It looks totally unoptimized.

Here’s another app that fills up 1/3 of the screen. Granted, I mostly use Uber on the cover display for booking rides, but Lyft has already updated and optimized its app — so it fills the big screen.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

Look, I’m not expecting an immersive LinkedIn experience when I use my iPhone Duo, but I’m not expecting a layout that looks outdated and broken. Pressing the rotate button fills up more of your screen, but it’s still not great. Maybe LinkedIn could post an app developer job ad…

I don’t have a major problem using the 5.4-inch cover display for ordering dinner. But I would at least like to have the option to use the bigger canvas for browsing menus, especially Cheesecake Factory.

There are some pretty great calendar apps for the iPhone Duo. Google Calendar is not one of them. For now I would download Fantastical. It offers a wide format on the big screen and lets you easily check the weather along with your schedule and keep track of your to-dos.

This isn’t the only banking app that hasn’t been updated for the iPhone Duo yet, but it’s annoying for me because it’s the one I use. Wells Fargo is fine on the front screen for checking your balance or doing a quick transfer, but not so much for reviewing purchases where it helps to have more real estate.

The Gmail app looks better than Drive and Sheets in that it actually fills the screen (yay!), but it doesn’t feature the 2-column layout that I would expect. So you can’t see your inbox on the left and your messages on the right as you can on Android foldables. It’s a massive waste of a 7.6-inch canvas.

Did you hear that Doordash is buying Instacart for $17 billion? Well, it appears that neither company can afford to optimize their apps for the iPhone Duo right now. You basically get the phone app slapped on a larger screen, which makes shopping and browsing more tedious than it needs to be.

While there are plenty of apps that look great on the iPhone Duo, too many apps are just not optimized yet. And while it’s not Apple’s responsibility to fix the problem, the longer this drags on the more excuses people will have not to splurge. I would be way more aggressive in cajoling developers to update their wares for this form factor.

Maybe app makers are waiting for a critical mass of iPhone Duo users, which is a chicken-and-egg scenario that may be hard to overcome — at least until Apple is able to keep up with demand for this device.

#3320. Hawaiian Electric (HE) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Storm costs and a wildfire settlement prepayment shaped the quarter.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Hawaiian Electric Industries, Inc. (HE -0.24%) is executing a strategic simplification of its business model by transitioning into a pure-play regulated electric utility following the initial public offering of its banking subsidiary and the liquidation of its non-regulated renewable energy assets. Management reported that the company has restored access to capital markets and maintained a liquidity position of $1.3 billion to manage multiyear wildfire settlement obligations and essential grid investments. The company is currently navigating a rate rebasing process and a regulatory review of its performance-based regulation framework while implementing a comprehensive wildfire mitigation plan that has contributed to a 52% reduction in commercial insurance premiums. The utility's strategy focuses on balancing affordability with necessary resilience investments through the use of state-authorized securitization and strategic divestitures aimed at achieving investment-grade credit metrics over the long term.

Operator: Thank you for joining us, and welcome to the HEI Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the conference over to Mateo Garcia, Director of Investor Relations. Sir, please go ahead.

Mateo Garcia: Thank you. Welcome, everyone, to HEI's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. Joining me today are our CEO, Scott Seu; our President, Shelee Kimura; our Senior Vice President and CFO, Paul Ito; and other members of senior management. Our earnings release and our presentation for this call are available in the Investor Relations section of our website. As a reminder, forward-looking statements will be made on today's call. Factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from expectations can be found in our presentation, our SEC filings and in the Investor Relations section of our website. Today's presentation also includes references to non-GAAP financial measures, including those referred to as core items.

You should refer to the information contained in the slides accompanying today's presentation for definitional information and reconciliations of historical non-GAAP measures to the closest GAAP financial measure. We will take questions from institutional investors at the end of this call. Individual investors and others can reach out to Investor Relations. Now Scott Seu will begin with his remarks.

Scott W. Seu: Aloha kakou. Welcome, everyone. For today's call, I'll start with updates on key strategic priorities and regulatory processes. Paul Ito will walk through the quarter's results and discuss the financial implications of pending regulatory requests. Throughout this year, we've continued to make measurable progress across the key objectives that we've communicated since the Maui wildfires of 2023. We told you that we would take the actions necessary to improve the financial strength of our enterprise and ensure our ability to serve and invest in our communities for the long term. Over the past 3 years, we've done this by improving our financial and operational risk profile, resulting in upgrades in both HEI and Hawaiian Electric's ratings from all 3 agencies.

Our liquidity today is more than 5x what it was just after the wildfires and more than twice what it was just before the wildfires, giving us significant optionality as we look ahead toward making the remaining payments stipulated under the historic settlement agreement that was upheld by the Hawaii Supreme Court earlier this year. We've also restored our access to capital, completing successful debt and equity offerings at the operating company level and holding company level, respectively. We've achieved substantial milestones in implementing our Wildfire Mitigation Plan, resulting in significantly lower risk of utility-caused ignitions across our system. The effectiveness of our efforts has not only been recognized by the rating agencies, but by our insurance providers as well.

Our insurers have recognized us as among the best-in-class with respect to wildfire risk mitigation. And as a result, our price per million for commercial wildfire premiums has declined 52% since the Maui wildfires. We're also implementing our Wildfire Mitigation Plan at the least cost to customers, with securitization planned to cover up to $500 million in wildfire mitigation program costs and other resilience spending. With the divestitures of American Savings Bank and the Pacific Current businesses, we're moving ahead with a more streamlined and simpler business solely focused on a regulated electric utility.

After consistently achieving aggressive strategic milestones to date under challenging circumstances, we're well positioned for strong execution of our strategies, ensuring that we can continue to strengthen the financial position of the company while serving our communities with safe, affordable, reliable and resilient electricity. Turning to the next slide. We continue to advance strategic priorities during the third quarter. Our islands experienced elevated storm activity in August and September, and I'm proud of the strong performance of our crews in quickly restoring power following severe weather and damage to our system. Hurricane Lala caused extensive statewide damage as it passed through the southern portion of the island chain in mid-August, causing hurricane force winds across the state.

At their peak, outages impacted over 40% of customer accounts across our service territories. However, our crews made rapid progress restoring service under challenging weather conditions, with more than 95% of affected customers restored within 3 days of the storm's passing. Hurricane Lowell passed by our service territories in early September, with limited impacts to our system. Our crews provided assistance to Kauai Island Utility Cooperative to restore power on the island of Kauai, which experienced severe impacts. In September, Hurricane Nolo had only minor impacts in our service territory, with a handful of outages that our crews quickly addressed. Most customers' power was restored within hours.

Our ability to quickly restore customers in the face of very challenging weather conditions is a result of the hard work of Hawaiian Electric crews and our effective execution implementing resiliency measures. The significant resources invested in resilience as we've implemented our Wildfire Mitigation Plan proved beneficial in the face of these severe weather events. For example, measures already implemented in high wildfire risk areas, such as pole upgrades and enhanced vegetation trimming, have resulted in fewer pole failures during extreme weather events. We continue to prioritize safety in everything we do, and we've implemented industry-wide best practices, adopting proven measures used by wildfire-affected utilities on the mainland, but tailored to our very different risk profile.

Hawaii's wildfire risk differs significantly from that of California or other wildfire-prone Western states, where large-scale wildfires are a regular occurrence, often numerous times a year. We continue to implement industry best practices to strengthen safety and reduce risk of utility equipment involvement in an ignition. Wildfire risk reduction has also become a statewide collaborative effort involving many dedicated parties beyond the state's utilities. Government agencies, first responders, landowners, nonprofits and others are engaged in dedicated efforts and have increased funding and other resources to reduce the risk of ignition, spread and impact of wildfires. Along with safety, reliability and resilience, affordability remains a priority in everything we do. Our pending rate rebasing request reflects that balance.

We've proposed a 5.3% base rate increase phased in over 2 years that is in line with projected inflation while supporting the continued investments needed for a safe, reliable and resilient grid. We're mindful of the cost pressures our customers face, especially our low-income customers, in the current high price environment. That's also why we recently sought PUC approval of up to $500 million in wildfire safety and resilience investments using securitization, which was authorized by Hawaii's legislature and signed into law by Governor Green last year. The structure is designed to lower the cost to customers while advancing public safety.

Our work to consistently deliver for our customers has not gone unrecognized, and we've seen consistent improvement in customer satisfaction over the past 3 years. We were pleased to see that customer satisfaction scores during the quarter remained well above industry averages, with customer satisfaction in the 86th percentile of over 100 utilities surveyed. Turning to the next slide. Our rate rebasing continues to progress. And over the past few months, public hearings have been held on all islands we serve. We are awaiting a final PUC procedural schedule, which will give us a better sense of the next significant milestone dates and when new rates might take effect.

In the meantime, the review process to consider PBR framework changes for the next 5 years is progressing toward conclusion. In October, the PUC issued guidance for what is called PBR Phase 6, including a staff proposal to narrow focus for the remaining steps in this process. The staff proposal is largely aligned with our own positions on PBR modifications. The collaboration and discussions among the PBR stakeholder parties to this point should facilitate a PUC decision on final PBR framework changes in the near future, although no time line for such a decision has been set thus far. We'll be filing our comments on the PUC staff's proposal no later than November 13.

The PUC has laid out high-level procedural steps following the reply comments, with the next major milestone being the commission's inclinations, expected to be published in early January. In summary, our key PBR-related regulatory processes are advancing, and we expect more clarity on the exact timing for conclusion of the rate rebasing and Phase 6 in the near term. We continue to execute on our operational priorities, maintaining our focus on affordability while delivering the safe, reliable and resilient electricity our customers deserve. I'll now turn the call over to Paul to discuss our financial results.

Paul Ito: Thank you, Scott. I'll start with our financial results on Slide 6. For the third quarter of 2026, we generated GAAP net income of $35.5 million or $0.20 per share compared to $30.7 million or $0.18 per share a year ago. The results include the impacts of several items we consider noncore. American Savings Bank completed an initial public offering in September. And as part of the transaction, HEI sold 35% of its 9.9% stake, realizing net proceeds of approximately $33.9 million and a pretax gain of $18.3 million. HEI also recognized a noncash unrealized gain of $45.9 million on its remaining stake in the bank, reflecting its market value at quarter end.

In total, the realized and unrealized gains were approximately $64 million pretax. We also recorded a noncash pretax asset impairment of $50.7 million at Pacific Current related to its last remaining operating asset, the Mahipapa biomass generating facility on Kauai. In September, the proposed sale of Mahipapa to an unaffiliated third party was terminated because the parties could not resolve certain obligations needed to close the sale. Mahipapa's facility has been offline since early September following damage from Hurricane Lowell, and its power purchase agreement with Kauai Island Utility Cooperative, or KIUC, ended on October 1. Mahipapa filed for Chapter 7 liquidation on November 3. Once the proceeding is completed, there will be no remaining operations under Pacific Current.

We've worked to minimize the impacts of the shutdown on stakeholders, including Mahipapa employees, KIUC and creditors. The impairment reduced the plant assets to their estimated net salvage value. Similar to last quarter, utility interest expense includes approximately $18 million of noncash accretion expense on the wildfire settlement liability. As a reminder, we discounted the remaining settlement payments to present value last quarter. Accretion increases that recorded liability as the payment dates approach. It does not increase the agreed settlement payments. Excluding ASB investment gains, the Pacific Current impairment and Maui wildfire-related items, consolidated core net income and EPS were $23 million and $0.13, down from $32.8 million and $0.19 in the third quarter of 2025.

The decline primarily reflects storm-related expenses at the utility, which remain included in both GAAP and core results. At the utility, GAAP net income was $13.5 million compared to $37 million a year ago. Utility core net income for the quarter was $27.6 million compared to $39.6 million in 2025. The decrease in utility core net income primarily reflects higher O&M expenses. The higher utility O&M was driven by $13.7 million of estimated incremental pretax storm costs related to hurricanes in August and September and approximately $5.6 million of expenses previously recorded at the holding company, but now recorded at the utility.

This transfer started in the third quarter and reflects the integration of holding company functions and employees into the utility as we simplify the business. The ongoing expenses are now recorded at the utility, but the transfer itself did not increase consolidated expenses. The costs that remain at the holding company will primarily consist of interest expense on holding company debt and holding company expenses that are unrelated to utility operations. In October, we filed for deferral of the storm-related expenses and have requested a PUC decision no later than December 15, 2026. If approved and the applicable accounting criteria are met, we would reverse the qualifying expenses in our fourth quarter financials.

Our request covers incremental, prudently incurred storm costs. We'll then file for recovery in a separate request to the PUC in 2027 under our Z-factor recovery mechanism. We believe the storm costs meet the required criteria specified for recovery under the Z-factor because the costs were prudently incurred, incremental and related to exogenous events outside of the control of the utility. Approval to defer the costs would not by itself constitute approval of recovery. Holding company core net loss for the quarter was $4.6 million compared to $6.8 million in the third quarter of 2025.

The lower core net loss was primarily driven by the holding company expenses that are now being recorded at the utility, partially offset by lower interest income due to a lower cash balance following the first settlement payment made in April of this year. Turning to the next slide. As of the end of the third quarter, on a consolidated basis, total liquidity was approximately $1.3 billion. This includes $224 million of unrestricted cash on hand and approximately $1.1 billion of liquidity available under HEI's ATM program, HEI's and the utility's credit facility capacity and the utility's accounts receivable facility.

We continue to believe that we are well positioned to meet increased working capital requirements due to higher fuel prices, as well as financing needs related to utility CapEx. Consistent with last quarter, we have not seen a meaningful increase in bad debt expense or write-offs this year, and bad debt expense is actually lower than it was at this time last year, while net write-offs have been relatively flat. Turning to the next slide. As Scott mentioned, our rate rebasing request is being reviewed by the PUC. The PUC's tentative procedural schedule contemplates a final decision in order in mid- to late April 2027. This could allow for new rates to take effect by early May.

Under this illustrative scenario, assuming our full rate rebasing requests were granted, we would see $83 million of additional revenue from the rate rebasing in 2027, which is 8 months of the full year run rate of $125 million. Under the scenario for a partial year of new rates, the utility would manage to a core return on equity of approximately 7.3% to 7.8%. That is equivalent to approximately 8.3% to 8.8% under a full year of new rates, reflecting the full $125 million base rate increase.

The partial year and full year ROE scenarios do not include the potential impacts from new performance incentive mechanisms or other changes to the PBR framework that are being considered under Phase 6 of the PBR proceeding. These scenarios are illustrative, and the timing and outcome of the PUC's decision remain uncertain. If the PUC approves the PIMs package proposed by the company in the Phase 6 PBR proceeding, the potential upside of up to 150 basis points of ROE in PIMs would be approximately $33 million. The potential downside from up to 50 basis points of ROE and PIM penalties would be approximately $11 million. Turning next to our financing plans.

Our strong quarter end liquidity provides significant flexibility as we look ahead toward funding our CapEx and the remaining wildfire settlement payments. We have already prepaid $80 million toward the second settlement payment, reducing the $479 million amount due by $82 million after reflecting the early payment discount. In addition, we expect to prepay at least another $100 million before the April 2027 due date using proceeds from the potential sale of our remaining shares of ASB and expected insurance proceeds. If completed as expected, these prepayments would reduce the amount remaining due in April to below $300 million. We still expect to finance the remainder of the second payment with straight debt or convertible debt.

We have a variety of financing options available, and with strong liquidity, we have flexibility on timing as market conditions evolve. We also have the option to make some or all of the remaining settlement payments early, with a discount applied based on an annualized rate of 5.5%. We will continue to evaluate additional prepayments against our financing costs and liquidity needs. Our financing strategy will focus on minimizing shareholder dilution while building toward investment-grade credit metrics over the long term. We believe achieving those metrics, together with the implementation of the wildfire protections contemplated by Act 258 and completion of the remaining settlement payments, would provide a credible path back to investment-grade.

The timing and outcome of any rating actions remain at the discretion of the rating agencies. As our financial position strengthens, our Board of Directors may revisit our dividend policy with a longer-term objective of reaching a payout ratio consistent with peer utilities. We'll now open up the call for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from Michael Lonegan with Barclays.

Michael Lonegan: So you talked about the early payment approach for the wildfire liabilities. So I was just wondering if you could share if you're leaning more towards -- for the remaining amount, more towards debt or convertible debt? And is this something you could expect in the near term or closer to the April due date for the PEP payment?

Paul Ito: Mike, this is Paul. So just to clarify, you're asking about the second settlement payment that's coming up specifically?

Paul Ito: Okay. Yes. So let me just start where we're at and what our plan is as we get to the April settlement payment date. So as I said on the call, we've already prepaid $80 million at a discount. And so that reduces the remaining amount to about $400 million. We expect to obtain additional proceeds to do a prepayment from our remaining ASB stake. And we also expect additional insurance proceeds. And so roughly speaking, that's a little bit over $100 million, and that would allow us to prepay to further reduce the amount to $300 million or slightly less.

In terms of the remaining $300 million and how we would finance that, our plans remain consistent with what we said before. It will be debt or convertible debt. We're looking at both. Obviously, we're watching market conditions. And we're going to look at the trade-offs between the two and then make a decision at the appropriate moment, but that's our current plan.

Michael Lonegan: And then I was wondering if you could talk about the status of the liability cap process, when we could expect updates on that? And could this potentially go through the -- in the next legislative session in 2027?

Scott W. Seu: Mike, this is Scott. So the process is still being overseen by the Public Utilities Commission. This is a formal rule-making process. They are in the midst of that. They have spent time seeking inputs from various stakeholders, including our company, and that's where it sits. The next step is really up to the PUC in terms of when they would be able to issue a set of draft rules for consideration. But obviously, that would be sometime in 2027.

Michael Lonegan: Okay. And then lastly for me, there are some tweaks to the 2027 and 2028 capital program. I was just wondering if you could walk us through what changed there? And then also, I know, like -- you've said the majority of your capital program will be funded with prior debt issuances and cash flow. Just -- do you expect to use your ATM much as well?

Paul Ito: So maybe I'll start with the ATM. Currently, based on where our stock price is, there's no plans to utilize that. As mentioned, currently, we don't pay a dividend. And so we would expect to fund largely our CapEx program through internally generated earnings, but also supplement that with debt. In terms of changes to the CapEx program, I don't believe there was a significant change. Sometimes there's a shifting of EPRM timing of the capital. But generally, it remains largely consistent, I believe, with last quarter.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I will now turn the call back to Scott Seu for closing remarks.
